# Working Papers

:::{.papers}
**[The Distributional Consequences of Net-Zero Transitions](papers/net-zero%20transition_manuscript.pdf){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"}** (with [Hakkı Yazıcı](https://hakkiyazici.net/)) · *Submitted*

> This paper studies the distributional consequences of net-zero transitions. Using an environmentally-extended input-output table linked with the U.S. Consumer Expenditure Survey, we show that the carbon intensity of expenditure declines with income, largely due to differences in energy expenditure shares. We develop a heterogeneous agent overlapping-generations model with non-homothetic preferences, estimated using household-level data, that matches key distributional moments of the U.S. economy. We evaluate a carbon tax path consistent with the U.S. net-zero target under the Paris Agreement. Although the reform disproportionately affects poorer households in the short run, lifetime welfare costs are similar across income groups. Across cohorts, those in their fifties when the reform is introduced experience the largest losses. We find that the time path of carbon taxes impacts the distributional consequences of climate reforms substantially. An optimal reform that maximizes average welfare almost fully coincides with the carbon tax path implied by the Paris Agreement.
:::

**Climate Change, Structural Change and Labour Market Displacement** (with [Ctirad Slavík](https://home.cerge-ei.cz/slavik/) and [Hakkı Yazıcı](https://hakkiyazici.net/))

> How are the welfare costs of carbon taxation distributed across the income distribution? We use a heterogeneous-agent framework with non-homothetic preferences to separate the direct expenditure burden from general-equilibrium effects on wages and capital returns.

**The Skill Premium Across Space**

> Place-based interventions can be welfare-improving from both an efficiency and equity perspective. However, most of what is known about the conditions for optimality relies on planners having access to location-specific taxes and transfers. In practice, income taxation is almost always place-blind, and place-based interventions take the form of targeted investment in amenity improvement, productivity enhancement, or efforts to alter housing supply elasticities. This paper takes a sufficient statistics approach to characterize the key elasticities governing optimality among this restricted set of policy instruments. I estimate these elasticities using the UK's Single Regeneration Budget (SRB): a collection of 950 local projects with heterogeneous objectives and spending, rolled out in a staggered fashion in the late-1990s and early-2000s. I take these elasticities to a quantitative spatial model, and allow for a wider set of tax instruments, as well as origin-destination specific migration frictions.
